abstractText:
This project seeks to understand the mechanisms that underlie the transition of a dynamical system from an ordered state to a random (chaotic) state. In other words, the aim is to understand the processes through which a system's behavior evolves from periodicity toward chaos, as one or more governing parameters are varied. A related goal is to identify the primary bifurcation responsible for qualitative changes exhibited by a dynamical system. While such comprehension has previously been attained for low-dimensional dynamical systems, this project introduces a novel approach to transcend the low-dimensional limitation. The project will offer new conceptual ideas and approaches to provide fresh perspectives on advances in mathematics and science. Additionally, the project will facilitate the training of graduate students directly engaged in the research, and will afford educational opportunities to undergraduate students through the organization of a summer school presenting topics in mathematics, including topics related to dynamical systems.

The theory of one-dimensional dynamical systems successfully explains the depth and complexity of chaotic phenomena in concert with a description of the dynamics of typical orbits for typical maps. Its remarkable universality properties supplement this understanding with powerful geometric tools. In the two-dimensional setting, the range of possible dynamical scenarios that can emerge is at present only partially understood, and a general framework for those new phenomena that do not occur for one-dimensional dynamics remains to be developed. In prior work supported by the NSF, the principal investigator introduced a large open class of two-dimensional dynamical systems, including the classical Henon family without the restriction of large area contraction, that is amenable to obtaining results as in the one-dimensional case. Moreover, major progress was reached to understand the transition from zero entropy to positive entropy using renormalization schemes. The present project has several components. First, existing renormalization schemes will be adapted to the positive entropy realm. Next, initial steps towards a characterization of dissipative diffeomorphisms in more general contexts will be addressed. Finally, the principal investigator will seek to develop the theory of differentiable renormalization without an a priori assumption of proximity to the one-dimensional setting. These results will open the door to a global description of dissipative diffeomorphisms and their behavior under perturbation, bringing both new tools and new perspectives to smooth dynamical systems theory.

This doctoral dissertation research investigates the decision-making, motivations, and variations amongst local and indigenous communities in the management of land and other natural resources. It specifically examines how local communities build and adapt sustainable solutions to changing environmental and political conditions.  The dissertation research project trains a graduate student in methods of scientific data collection and analysis. Findings will be disseminated in various public venues to help the public understand the ways local and diverse communities and their needs can be included in adaptations to global energy and resource transitions. 

To analyze how and why various stakeholders in local communities manage natural resources and decision-making the investigators use systematic spatial land-mapping, geological data, impact assessments, and ethnographic methods. Findings from this study contribute to the scholarship in environmental anthropology, studies of land use, and geology.

projectOutComesReport:
This research investigates how Indigenous and rural communities in southwest Bolivia respond to the expansion of lithium mining in the Uyuni Salt Flat — the world’s largest salt desert and a key site in the global energy transition. While lithium is essential for batteries and renewable energy systems, its extraction from brine poses significant social, political, and environmental challenges in ecologically fragile regions where communities depend on scarce water resources.

The research examines how local actors navigate overlapping land claims, scientific uncertainty, and the political stakes of large-scale extractive development. It addresses three core questions:

  1. How does scientific uncertainty regarding geology, hydrology, and environmental risk shape governance and public decision-making?
  2. How do Indigenous and rural communities articulate territorial claims, identity-based demands, and political participation in the face of state-led lithium industrialization?
  3. How is environmental knowledge produced by communities and their allies — including engineers, lawyers, and NGOs — to contest official narratives and advance alternative visions of development?

To address these questions, the project combined ethnographic fieldwork with document analysis and environmental monitoring. Twelve months of research in Bolivia included interviews with scientists, engineers, community leaders, and government officials; participation in Indigenous councils and public forums; and collaborative water testing in wetlands surrounding the salt flat. Archival research was conducted at the Bolivian Geological Service (GEOBOL) to trace how evidence of lithium reserves has been historically produced. Additional research in historical archives in Potosí, Sucre, and Seville focused on the political, demographic, and territorial construction of the region, including the historical foundations of identity and land claims.

Findings reveal that scientific uncertainty — including limited hydrological data and the variable chemistry of brines — plays a central role in shaping territorial disputes and weakening the legitimacy of official assessments. In this context, competing interpretations of risk, sustainability, and extraction become tools of political negotiation.

The research also documented how communities, often excluded from formal decision-making, are generating their own environmental knowledge. Through collaborations with NGOs and technical allies, they have engaged in community-based water monitoring, legal mapping of land rights, and the creation of locally relevant environmental indicators. These efforts not only challenge official expertise but also reflect broader attempts to define sustainability on their own terms.

Additionally, the study revealed ongoing tensions between the state’s authority over the Uyuni Salt Flat—designated as a fiscal reserve for lithium extraction—and the territorial claims of Indigenous populations and peasant unions in the surrounding region. Various actors have mobilized scientific and historical evidence to assert their longstanding connection to the land and to seek legal and political recognition. These dynamics underscore the complex intersections of geology, governance, and identity in Bolivia’s lithium frontier.

Beyond contributing new empirical insights, the project advances theoretical debates in environmental anthropology, political ecology, and science and technology studies by analyzing how extractive governance is shaped by scientific uncertainty, contested epistemologies, and conflicting territorial histories. It offers one of the first in-depth ethnographic accounts of Bolivia’s lithium frontier and foregrounds the role of grassroots knowledge in shaping the politics of energy transitions. The project also supported interdisciplinary collaboration among communities, legal advocates, and technical professionals, producing outcomes that are relevant not only to academic audiences but also to local stakeholders and policymakers seeking more inclusive and sustainable approaches to environmental governance.

This project provides continuing support for U.S. participation in LIS, the cross-national data archive and research center. LIS is an indispensable, multi-country data infrastructure for understanding the social and economic wellbeing of people in today’s globalized world. LIS maintains two social science databases—the Luxembourg Income Study (LIS) Database and the Luxembourg Wealth Study (LWS) Database—for the purposes of enabling and fostering cross-national research on socio-economic outcomes in high- and middle-income countries. The current project adds new datasets to both the LIS and LWS Databases on a continual basis. The project also includes a pilot study on including top-end adjustments to the income and wealth series, as well as an assessment of the feasibility of a new database, tentatively titled the “Luxembourg Consumption Study (LCS) Database,” populated with consumption datasets from many countries. Thousands of researchers worldwide—10,000 to date—use the LIS and LWS Databases to analyze outcomes including poverty, household income outcomes, employment disparities, family structure, wealth portfolios, asset levels, and the interplay between household income and wealth. This ever-growing body of research informs decision-making about income and wealth distributions in the United States and around the world.

The project harmonizes datasets from many countries, which include microdata on income, wealth, employment, and demography; provides a means to access data that would otherwise be unavailable to individual researchers due to privacy restrictions; creates a remote-execution system that quickly sends research query results back to users off-site; and promotes the use of microdata in comparative research on socio-economic wellbeing. By providing an infrastructure with data from geographically and economically diverse countries, LIS broadens the intellectual basis for interdisciplinary research using household microdata. LIS maintains the Luxembourg Income Study (LIS) Database and the Luxembourg Wealth Study (LWS) Database, which together cover more than 80% of the world’s GDP and 2/3 of its population. LIS acquires, harmonizes, and documents survey-based datasets from around the globe; these include income, employment, and demographic variables at the person- and household-level. The LIS Database includes microdata from 55 countries, with nearly 700 datasets spanning 1968 to 2019; the newer LWS Database contains 75 wealth datasets from 19 countries and covers 1995 to 2019. LIS maintains standardized national indicators on household income and poverty, and metadata are available on the surveys, harmonization, and country-specific institutions. LIS provides online learning materials, user support, and training workshops, as well as a Working Paper Series, a Visiting Scholar Program, LIS-based conferences, and public programs. LIS serves thousands of researchers worldwide, from various disciplines, including economics, sociology, political science, policy studies, and public health. Users come from academia, government agencies, non-governmental organizations, supranational organizations, and news agencies; over one-fifth of registered and active users are based in the United States. The current project continues to broaden LIS’ impact beyond academia by expanding collaborations, communicating through various media, and continuing to enhance its data visualization capacity.

This award provides partial support for early career US-based mathematicians to attend the conference "Random matrices from quantum chaos to the Riemann zeta function’’.  This meeting will take place at the University of Bristol on 5–7th July 2023.  The conference will focus on highlighting recent mathematical achievements, spanning topics from Analytic Number Theory, to Quantum Chaos, to Random Matrix Theory.  This award will facilitate interaction between early career mathematicians and the leading experts in the field. 

Half a century ago, mathematicians discovered that various behaviors of the Riemann zeta function can accurately be predicted by particular large Hermitian random matrices. In the intervening years, ideas from quantum chaos, statistical physics, probability, combinatorics, and more, have furthered our understanding of the Riemann zeta function and other L-functions. One of the most recent advances has been the significant progress towards the Fyodorov-Keating conjecture(s) concerning extreme values of the Riemann zeta function and of characteristic polynomials. This conference will bring together experts working at these interfaces alongside early career researchers, and provide ample opportunity for learning and discussion.

The conference: "Random matrices from quantum chaos to the Riemann zeta function. A celebration in honour of Jon Keating's 60th birthday" took place between July 5th and July 7th 2023 at the University of Bristol. The conference comprised 14 1-hour talks and 1 public lecture, with speakers representing 13 global institutions.  The conference featured over 140 attendees, including PhD students, postdoctoral researchers, early-career mathematicians, and established field leaders.  The speakers, and their topics, were chosen to represent the diverse range of mathematics that Prof. Keating has contributed to during his career to date.


The award was instrumental in supporting 7 graduate students and early-career researchers to attend the conference. All participants enjoyed talks from seemingly disparate mathematical areas including random matrix theory, probability, quantum chaos, number theory, dynamical systems, and mathematical physics. Feedback from the participants confirms that all talks were to an exceedingly high-level, engaging, and thought-provoking.  The opportunity to learn from and engage with such established researchers is fundamental for early-career mathematicians, aiding them to widen both their research community and mathematical frontiers.  Again, the success of this aim was evidenced through feedback post-conference, with attendees noting in particular that the conference had plenty of opportunities to network and discuss the new mathematical ideas.

abstractText:
Humans have different kinds of knowledge about the languages they speak. Phonotactic knowledge refers to their knowledge about sound patterns in words. Such knowledge is usually studied through behavioral experiments such as wordlikeness judgment tasks, in which a speaker is asked to indicate whether a nonce (made-up) word form could be a real word in their language. Such studies have observed that wordlikeness judgements are gradient; that is, they form a cline of acceptability.  This project examines different types of computational models and experimental designs to better understand the nature of the grammatical system that underly this variety of gradient judgment.  For example, one class of computational models seek to account for this gradience in wordlikeness tasks by incorporating fine-grained generalizations in sophisticated statistical models.  In contrast, other models based solely on categorical generalizations appear to do just as well in accounting for behavioral wordlikeness findings. This suggests that gradience observed in the behavioral experiments may reflect the experimental setting rather than the underlying grammar of the knowledge itself. This collaborative research project develops a thorough investigation of these contrasting accounts of gradience in human wordlikeness judgements. The project provides mentoring and research training opportunities for graduate students in modern experimental and computational methods; and it creates an open-access, online database of the project's experimental results that serves as a resource for other researchers in the language sciences. In addition, the investigators plan to engage in outreach activities targeting members of the public in settings focusing on informal science education.

This research project deconstructs the variety of factors involved in wordlikeness judgements. It includes experimental studies that manipulate response measures and stimulus and response modality to elicit human-subjects' wordlikeness judgments for nonce forms from speakers of English and Korean.  A variety of computational models are assessed by comparing how well they can be fitted to the results of the experimental studies. The project's interconnected studies aim to answer the following questions: (a) how do different explicit computational models perform against observed wordlikeness judgments, (b) to what degree is gradience in acceptability judgments related to the probabilistic nature of human perception, and (c) are the results obtained affected by the manner in which words forms are presented to speakers (e.g., auditorily vs. visually) and/or in which speakers record their judgments?

This project will provide partial support for the conference "Theoretical Biophysics: Searching for principles" (the Conference), to be held at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York City on Sep. 14 -16, 2022. The Conference will bring together world leaders in theoretical biophysics, and it will provide the opportunity for them to interact with education experts in the field, as well as with notable theorists in other fields of physics. The Conference is aimed at surveying achievements at the interface of theoretical physics and biology, to understand whether we expect theory at this interface to be different compared to the rest of theoretical physics, and if it will contribute differently, then how and why. Finally, the Conference will aim to understand challenges and opportunities involved in teaching the next generation of scientists at this interface.

The field of theoretical biophysics has grown in the recent decades from a boutique corner of physics to a substantial part of the international physics community. For example, over the course of the past ten years, the footprint of biophysics at the Annual March Meeting of the American Physical Society has more than doubled. Together with related fields of statistical physics (soft matter, polymer physics, statistical physics) biophysics now accounts for about a quarter of the talks at the meeting. Collectively, these groups are responsible for essentially all of the growth of the meeting in the last decade. Following such a rapid growth, it is now the time to take stock of the field and to understand where we are, and where we go from there. Are we still a single field, or have we fragmented into a collection of sub-disciplines roughly paralleling major divisions of life sciences? What have we contributed to understanding life that biologists would not be able to do on their own? Have we changed the discourse and the type of questions that are being asked? How do we educate the next generation of scientists to ensure that future progress remains equally dramatic?  This Conference is needed precisely to answer these questions. The conference will be timely since conferences in this area have been mostly virtual during the pandemic and the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine has just completed the first Decadal Review of Biological Physics

This event will provide an unparalleled opportunity to survey and summarize the current state of the field of theoretical biophysics. The perspectives presented at the Conference should help frame big questions for the next decade in the field. The presentations at the meeting will be recorded and made publicly available, increasing broader impact. Finally, by means of attracting a diverse group of participants, presenters, and discussants, including junior scientists, the meeting will contribute to the growth of diversity in physical sciences.

This award funds the research activities of Professor Vladimir Rosenhaus at The Graduate Center of the City University of New York.

Chaos, a ubiquitous phenomenon in nature, is the extreme sensitivity to small changes which gives rise to the violent churning inside of a smoke plume or behind a rock in a rapidly flowing river. The goal of this project is to better understand how chaos manifests itself at the smallest scales in nature, at the level of fundamental particles. A web of discoveries over the past decade, at the intersection of high energy physics, condensed matter physics, and quantum information theory, have revealed the essential role chaos must play in the eventual solution of one of the deepest problems in physics, of reconciling gravity with quantum mechanics. As a result, research in this area advances the national interest by promoting the progress of science in one of its most fundamental directions: the discovery and understanding of new physical laws. Professor Rosenhaus will search for signatures of chaos in theoretical computations of high energy particle scattering and will develop new models exhibiting many-body quantum chaos. This project is also envisioned to have significant broader impacts. Professor Rosenhaus will mentor graduate students and postdocs who will be involved in the research, develop new special topics graduate courses based on the research, give public lectures, and organize scientific workshops. 

More technically, Professor Rosenhaus will use chaos as a guide and a theme to better understand the dynamics of quantum field theories, and will study chaos in scattering in quantum field theory. The erratic behavior of many-particle scattering will provide the basis for a new measure of chaos in quantum field theory, which will shed light on nearly-integrable quantum field theories. In the context of string theory, he will compute novel scattering amplitudes of highly excited strings, giving a concrete demonstration of chaos in high energy scattering. In addition, building on the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model, new large N models exhibiting many-body quantum chaos will be found and used to gain insight on thermalization and chaos in strongly coupled quantum field theories. Through use of solvable models and conformal field theory techniques, novel examples of quantum turbulent cascades will be found.

The living world provides many fascinating examples of highly evolved, sophisticated machinery working in synergy to sustain life. A fundamental understanding of nature’s architectures and processes can be applied to create new biology-inspired and green technologies for the benefit of human and environmental health. However, this challenging task requires integrating aspects of research in biology, chemistry, and physics focused down to the smallest functional scale: the nanoscale. This NSF Research Traineeship (NRT), "Nanoscience Connected to Life: an Interdisciplinary Traineeship Program in Bioinspired Nanotechnology," will provide education, research, and career development to help build a new workforce in the emerging field of bioinspired nanotechnology. As this field undergoes rapid expansion and industry embraces these new approaches, society needs a uniquely trained and diverse workforce. Building on the City University of New York’s (CUNY) reputation as an engine for upward mobility of a diverse student population, this traineeship will provide a novel and comprehensive graduate education for 125 graduate students. The program will serve 25 directly funded trainees, including individuals from minority populations underrepresented in their pursuit of STEM fields of study, women, and members of the LGBTQ+ community. Graduates will become effective leaders who will be able to solve complex problems facing the U.S. and provide new scientific breakthroughs in energy harvesting, agriculture, medicine, and environmental remediation.   
 
The broad educational vision of this project is to train a generation of STEM Ph.D. students as collaborative, systems-level thinkers who can translate concepts across scales and disciplines. The project strengthens and integrates chemistry, biochemistry, and physics Ph.D. programs at CUNY through convergence around common goals. Students will become well-positioned to work on convergent teams to address urgent societal challenges related to environmental instabilities and health crises. At the heart of each student’s experience is a use-inspired project in one of several different areas of research employing biology-inspired approaches. These include: i) harvesting and conversion of energy, ii) designing nanoscale interfaces to measure and influence living systems, iii) newly designed sustainable green materials, and iv) development of adaptive metabolic systems and functional materials for therapeutic and industrial use. These investigations will span theoretical, computational, and experimental approaches. The project will prepare CUNY Ph.D. students for STEM careers in industrial, government, academic, and entrepreneurial tracks by integrating career awareness throughout the training period. The training plan is based on an innovative Integrating Mental Models and Experimental Research in Scientific Education (IMMERSE) training model, designed to create a learning community of systems thinkers. In this model, participants exchange knowledge and communicate across unfamiliar concepts, cultures, and methods. The IMMERSE training model can be replicated at other universities and in other convergent research areas.  
 
The NSF Research Traineeship (NRT) Program is designed to encourage the development and implementation of bold, new potentially transformative models for STEM graduate education training. The program is dedicated to effective training of STEM graduate students in high priority interdisciplinary or convergent research areas through comprehensive traineeship models that are innovative, evidence-based, and aligned with changing workforce and research needs.

The two primary objectives of this REU Site are 1) have a diverse population of undergraduate scholars conduct scientifically significant research in the fields of earth sciences, planetary sciences, and astrophysics; and 2) train and educate scholars in the fundamentals of the scientific enterprise in an inclusive, immersive, and supportive research and education environment. The Division of Physical Sciences at the American Museum of Natural History (AMNH), encompassing the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences and the Department of Astrophysics, is an ideal and unique facility to host this REU Site, with:

  • More than 25 active Ph.D.-level research scientists as potential mentors, representing a wide range of scientific interests and extensive experience in mentoring students and teaching;
  • A suite of in-house research resources including laboratories, computing power, physical and data collections, and extensive research library;
  • A fully integrated educational enterprise surrounding and supporting research, including the Richard Gilder Graduate School (RGGS) offering the Ph.D. in Comparative Biology and the Master of Arts in Teaching, Earth Science;
  • Public education resources including the Rose Center for Earth and Space, the Hayden Planetarium, and the Museum itself, with millions of visitors a year;
  • A location in the heart of the largest and most culturally diverse urban center in America, providing a safe and enjoyable big-city experience for rural and smaller-town students and easy accessibility for urban students.

This REU Site completed its twenty-second summer of operation in 2024 with stunning success as we regrouped following the turmoil of covid. From a program of six students per year in 2003-2005, we have supported up to 9 students per year 2006-2024, and now regularly host nearly 30 students annually in our “extended REU Site” anchored by the NSF REU program. In 2006, we also formalized the collaboration between AMNH and the City University of New York (CUNY) – the largest urban public university system in the nation with nearly a quarter million students in 25 colleges, all of which primarily serve urban and economically disadvantaged students, and 10 of which are identified as Minority Serving Institutions. Our partnership brings a strong New York City focus to our nationwide efforts and has increased our reach to underserved student populations.

Directly addressing our Intellectual Merit goals for this period, 5 research publications with recent REU student co-authors have appeared in peer-reviewed journals so far (an REU from 2020, now in the Physics PhD program at CUNY, has co-authored 15 peer-reviewed articles since 2022). Also, many more students presented at national meetings of the American Astronomical Society, the American Geophysical Union, the Geological Society of America, and the Lunar and Planetary Science Conference, plus others. While many of the students in the most recent cohorts are still completing their degrees, 6 are in graduate programs, one of which earned a Kavli post-baccalaureate before starting their PhD. A 2020 REU, now in the Astrophysics PhD program at Columbia, was recently awarded an NSF Graduate Research Fellowship.

Directly addressing our Broader Impact goals, during this 3-yr award period we attracted almost 1,000 applications (454 in 2024 alone) and selected 25 students from a wide variety of home institutions with limited or no research experience or opportunities, including community colleges, and with varied family histories with higher education. The REU also serves as a robust and seasoned training ground for mentors who are new faculty, postdocs, and grad students, some of which were REU scholars from our own site.

How individuals adjust identity to social change is an important question, as such adjustments affect how individuals understand their place within larger social and political structures. Social change offers opportunities to clarify fundamental tensions in modern societies between individualism versus collectivism and between private versus communal property. This doctoral dissertation research investigates whether and how visual media reflect and/or drive social change in rapidly changing socio-economic landscapes. The work provides a unique lens for investigating these dynamic feedbacks in ways that illustrate whether, how, and at what pace expressions of identity change in relation to larger socio-economic structures. The research contributes to training a U.S. doctoral student and its findings will be distributed widely to diverse audiences. 

Specifically, the project investigates what the economic and aesthetic strategies of contemporary visual media reveal about the socio-economic role of creative work in societies undergoing fundamental social and economic transformations. It considers whether and how concepts of property are exposed and reworked in the self-presentation, material production, and exhibition infrastructures of visual media during periods of rapid social change. Using an integration of ethnographic and archival methods, the doctoral student examines regional visual media as they respond to recent domestic socio-economic reforms in a context where transitions between collectivist and individualist notions of belonging are shifting. The student integrates direct observation, analysis of printed material, as well as interviews with relevant stakeholders to understand how regional visual media have responded to changes in property legislation following privatizing reforms. The results of this research provide a more robust account of visual media as both a barometer of and participant in processes of social, political-economic, and cultural change.

How individuals adjust identity to social, political, and economic change is an important question, as such adjustments affect how individuals understand their place within larger social and political structures. Dramatic social change offers opportunities to clarify fundamental tensions in modern societies. This doctoral dissertation research investigated whether and how visual media reflect and/or drive change in rapidly changing social landscapes. The work provides a unique lens for investigating these dynamic feedbacks in ways that illustrate whether, how, and at what pace expressions of identity change in relation to larger socio-political structures.

Specifically, this project, based in Havana, Cuba, investigated what the economic and aesthetic strategies of contemporary visual media reveal about the socio-economic role of creative work in a society undergoing fundamental political and economic transformations. A principal finding of this project is that the figure of the artist has been both a barometer of and participant in revolutionary Cuba's changing understandings of individuals' socio-political identities. This project arrived at its findings using a combination of ethnographic, archival, and interpretive methods. It integrates participant-observation, the analysis of printed and visual materials, as well as over fifty interviews with stakeholders in Cuba and in the diaspora. This research's aim is to consider how changing understandings of the artist correspond to and/or diverge from changing expectations for individuals over the course of Cuba's socialist history, with particular attention given to the present-day.

The intellectual merit of this project lies in its contribution to anthropological knowledge in three principal areas: identity, (post)socialism, and global artworlds.

Identity: Visual artists form a small sector of society that has depended, since at least the early 1990s, on individual resourcefulness and personal transnational networks for economic survival, a reality which has only been exacerbated during the current economic crisis. An important finding of this project is that today's Cuban artists show a hyper-individualism more typically associated with capitalist contexts. This hyper-individualism is in spite of a long history of socialist thought and pedagogy that posited visual artists as important intellectual workers for imagining a more collectively oriented society. This finding expands anthropological knowledge of individualism as experienced outside of Western, capitalist contexts.

(Post)socialism: This project analyzes a generalized sense of disappointment in a society which has long lost hope in a socialist future (to which the state is still nominally committed). And increasingly, as Cubans look to the predicaments of many formerly socialist and/or recently democratized postcolonial societies, the future of liberal democracy doesn't seem so bright either. Cuban artists' diverse roles over socialist Cuba's 64-year history are particularly illuminating- they have been the darlings of an imagined socialist future; the initial beneficiaries of Cuba's limited forays into a global market-system; among the loudest anti-government activists, and, more recently, some of the more caustic voices of apolitical cynicism. This analysis contributes to the extensive anthropological record on (post)socialist societies undergoing social, political, and economic transformation, while also opening a space for questioning whether (post)socialism continues to be a useful concept.

Global artworlds: This project participates in efforts to shift anthropological inquiry into art away from "traditional" aesthetic practices towards the contemporary, globalized artworld. Many scholars assert that today's artworld cannot be properly understood without paying attention to the massive impact of conceptualism. This research traces conceptualism's trajectory in Cuba, focusing on pedagogical methods and shifting state cultural policy. This historical research is complemented by ethnographic attention to conceptualism's enduring influence in higher arts education, widely shared art ideals, and institutional infrastructures in today's Cuba. Showing how conceptualism's legacy is experienced by artists confronting the tensions and contradictions inherent to a changing society enriches our understanding of the role elite cultural expressions play in broader social processes.

This project is posed to make a broader impact in two areas: 1.) public cultural programming in the US and 2.) US-Cuba cultural and academic exchange. This research allowed for the co-Principal Investigator (co-PI) to develop relationships with independent curators and culture sector public servants with extensive experience exhibiting Cuban artworks outside the island. The co-PI is currently working on two proposals for ethno-historical exhibitions which would broaden the US public's understanding of Cuban cultural life. The independence afforded by NSF funding facilitated connections with a variety of private cultural initiatives, as well as state-run cultural institutions. The ties established as part of this research will be mobilized for the benefit of expanded academic and cultural exchange between the United States and Cuba.

abstractText:
This doctoral dissertation research project investigates contemporary means of recording and accounting for ownership and responsibility by exploring cattle ranchers’ use of technology in animal husbandry. The researcher will focus on U.S. ranches that have adopted blockchain, the record-keeping mechanism underlying cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin. Agriculture is among the first sectors of the U.S. economy to implement blockchain in real-world cases unrelated to cryptocurrency. Historically, ranchers have proven ownership and controlled movement of cattle through a combination of branding and barbed wire, both of which had significant social impacts beyond cattle husbandry. Beef producers are now testing blockchain’s promise of making detailed transactional information publicly available, aiming to enable consumers to self-verify the provenance and quality of their food rather than placing trust in often opaque supply chains. This project, which trains a graduate student in methods of scientific data collection and analysis, explores the motivations and potential social ramifications of cutting-edge technology adoption. 

The project tests the hypothesis that the infrastructure of meat production is primarily organized around notions of risk. Some uncertainties inherent to food production, such as weather, are practically impossible to predict; others, such as predation loss or negligence liability, are to a greater extent predictable. Predictable losses can be quantified as risk and thus managed through insurance or other means of transfer. The investigator will perform observational research among cowhands, conduct interviews with lawmakers and technology promoters, and undertake archival research, inquiring into the context and motivation for the use of branding, barbed wire, and blockchain as provenance technologies that increase certainty of ownership. This inquiry will reveal the distribution of risk across the beef supply chain, including who bears the burdens of risk and who is able to leverage it to generate value. The research will contribute to a greater understanding of how risk is conceived of and commodified. The far-reaching impacts of such an understanding include the safety of the US meat supply, the general configuration of supply chains, and the relationship between agricultural innovation and notions of ownership and responsibility with respect to property.

This award ultimately went unused due to circumstances that prevented any research activity from being carried out during the funding period. Despite the initial plans for the project, no formal studies, experiments, or data collection began. The principal investigator originally intended to launch the research project shortly after the award was granted; however, a series of scheduling delays, resource limitations, and unforeseeable and unavoidable personal obligations made it impossible to establish the research framework in time. As a result, the project remained in its planning stage throughout the duration of the grant.

 

The principal investigator was unable to secure a research site and complete other necessary prerequisites and required approvals to initiate the study. Without these foundations in place, it was not feasible to start the work before the grant period and related extensions concluded. Once the funding timeline approached its expiration date, it became clear that the research could not proceed as originally envisioned. Consequently, the award expired without any research being formally undertaken under its provisions.

 

This unfortunately outcome was ultimately due to a misalignment between research readiness and funding timelines. Although the award provided a valuable opportunity, timing and other logistical challenges prevented the project from moving forward, and the grant ultimately went unused.

This doctoral dissertation project investigates collaboration between industries that typically operate outside the sphere of traditional finance. It focuses on the financial obstacles encountered by these industries, as well as how alliances among non-traditional industries allow these to be overcome. Specifically, using linguistic and cultural anthropological approaches, the research examines what role digital currency plays in facilitating financial market access among marginalized workers, as well as what beliefs and experiences most directly shape moral and economic notions of value within these transactional spaces. Research findings will be broadly disseminated to professionals, policy makers, and researchers in relevant fields and will include public outreach efforts to support the well-being of marginalized communities. Additionally, the research contributes to the training of a U.S.-based graduate student. 

Through a combination of in-person and digital ethnographic fieldwork at corporate offices and within the broader community of financially marginal individuals, as well as semiotic, social network, and other methods of data analysis, the project examines the economic, political and ethical motivations of this collaboration as well as its material and symbolic impacts. The researcher will conduct digital archival research to trace the financial and moral discourses that have shaped the margins of the finance industry and conduct interviews with users of alternate forms of financial transaction. The research builds on multiple anthropological literatures to provide a fresh perspective on how moral, monetary, and meaning-making practices interact in the creation and discernment of value.

Esra Padgett has completed research for her dissertation, “Technologies of Transaction in Moral Economic Framework” supported by the NSF Doctoral Dissertation Research Grant. During her funding period, she spent 12 months in Los Angeles conducting participant observation at the offices of a cryptocurrency company. As an anthropologist, Padgett was interested in understanding how novel financial technologies can be made useful to marginalized workers experiencing exclusion from mainstream financial institutions. Using linguistic and cultural anthropological approaches, the research specifically focused on the shared marginality of a legally marginal currency and a group of marginalized workers in order to advance understandings of financial access for disenfranchised communities as well as the study of moral and economic notions of value.

 

As a participant observer, Padgett accomplished the goal of her research and assisted in creating documentation materials to create a bridge between academia and public activism. By sharing research materials, including interviews with marginalized workers experiencing financial discrimination, she has helped create a resource for future public outreach. The data collected during this period is the foundation for an argument Padgett is formulating about the relationship between economic marginality, cultural stigma, and ethical decision-making. Through years of financial exclusion, marginalized workers have not only become hyper-knowledgeable about financial tools, but often serve as the test cases for emergent technologies. Many of these workers believe that banking should be a human right and have begun to organize around this issue in formal legal contexts.

 

Padgett also travelled to Las Vegas, Miami and Washington D.C. during her grant period to observe trade conventions, industry meet-ups and congressional fly-ins. The Miami trip centered around a tradeshow where the cryptocurrency company’s first product, a payment processor, was introduced to an industry experiencing financial discrimination. Padgett was able to observe how the marginalized laborers first using a novel financial tool help shape a product through feedback and initial trials. During the trip to D.C., Padgett observed as workers with histories of financial discrimination spoke with congress people on the issue of fair banking. Padgett’s involvement extends beyond her own research interests, and she helped draft the formal letter to congress members for this lobbying trip. In both trips, cultural and ethical notions of value were integral to the financial devaluation of these laborers, as they became marginalized by financial institutions despite working in legal businesses.

 

Padgett’s research over the course of the grant period forms the basis of her dissertation. The research is an important contribution to multiple anthropological literatures as it provides a fresh perspective on how moral, monetary and meaning-making practices interact in the creation and discernment of value and will be completed in 2024.

abstractText:
Many researchers consider social identities such as race and gender to be socially constructed categories. This allows researchers to understand these identities in light of their history, complexity, and relationships to each other. However, the practical application and use of social identities as socially constructed “objects of study” is uncommon in some fields of social science research. This project examines the research practices of experimental social psychologists. These researchers typically study the impact of the social environment on human behavior in a controlled laboratory setting. Despite some criticism, many social psychologists treat social identity categories as fixed, discrete objects to study them experimentally. These same types of studies are also criticized for other reasons, including lack of replicability and ease of fabrication. This project will investigate how social psychologists characterize and use social identity categories in their work, which may provide useful insights to address these critiques. Further, this research is important because the results of social psychology studies exert influence over decision-making in education, social and public policy, and the law. 

The primary objectives are to: 1) investigate the theories informing how social identity groups are understood and utilized in experiments, 2) analyze the methods research teams in social psychology use to select their focus of study; 3) offer first-hand accounts of how researchers’ identities affect their research products; and 4) analyze the impact and reach of social psychological experimental data. To meet these objectives, I will conduct ethnographic observations, interviews, and content analyses. Observations will allow documentation and analysis of social psychology researchers’ processes and practices in the laboratory. It will also illuminate how disciplinary culture and training affect the use of social identity. Interviews will lead to deeper understanding of the connection between researchers and their objects of study, and of how researchers view theories of social identity. Tracking and analysis of highly cited studies and the public presence of research findings (e.g., a lab’s social media postings) will form proxies of the societal impact of the research being studied. Ultimately, this project aims to improve the science of social identity and illuminate the ways information about certain social groups, which gets produced through scientific practice, shapes how those groups are characterized in public domains.

projectOutComesReport:
The stated aims of this dissertation were to gain understanding of the role of disciplinary culture, materials, and training in the theoretical orientations social psychologists maintain about the social identity groups in their scientific work; to gain insight into the relationship between researchers’ personal identity/lived experiences and their choices with regard to the treatment of social identity in their scientific work; and to examine how lab-based productions of social identity influence or shape public discourse(s) around social identity.
            The discipline of social psychology and its investigative practices, disseminated through mentorship and training, played a large role in the way individual psychologists and their research labs dealt with social identity-related variables. Though the theoretical perspective and orientation behind their understanding of the nature of social groups was not always well stated—and did not show any consensus, at least among the social psychologists and graduate students in the sample—researchers were able to narrate their social identity practices with ease. Both the analytical conventions exhibited by researchers as well as the scientific negotiations of the individual researchers in relation to how to treat social identity were affected by their understanding of the disciplinary requirements of social psychology. Academic and professional mentorship facilitated that certain research practices be passed down to current graduate students working under the primary investigators I interviewed. In addition to their training, personal life experiences and history also influenced how researchers understood and dealt with social identity. Everything from being a parent to being an immigrant influenced how researchers both engaged scientific practices and assessed the import of their work with social identity, even if they did not treat it as complexly as one would imagine given their personal experiences with the social identity categories they study. Interestingly, in instances where researchers articulated they had no specific personal connection(s) to their objects of study, interviews revealed that there were still intrusions of personal history into the lab space, mainly through the presence and impact of family members who held the particular social identities being investigated in the researchers’ work, or work of the students they supervised.
            The text network analysis illuminated the social identity-based interactions between academic and nonacademic texts. Categories and associated claims about categories were treated differently across both types of texts and initial patterns emerged in terms of how journalists and lawyers used scientific information to validate desired social identity claims for their own purposes. Scientific literature emerged as an additional way to validate lay claims about social groups in society in lieu of being a sole source of expertise or influence on the way nonacademic writers spoke about social identity categories in their writing.
            Given the data from the interviews and lab observations, social psychologists would do well to think critically about how disciplinary socialization impacts their scientific practices and, specifically, notions of experimental need for objectivity. At present the disciplinary conventions around experimentation haunt social psychological innovations and restrict what is seen as possible or feasible by researchers—they limit how social groups are understood and ultimately how they are rendered available to be used within the narrow parameters prescribed by the experimental paradigm. The discipline, as a part of its function in the broader academy, requires scientists to move quickly, to define simply (or not define at all), and to flatten the complexities of identity as they exist both inside and outside of persons.
            With relation to the uptake of scientific publications produced by social psychologists, it seems to me that there should be a process of complicating notions of access to social psychological information and dissemination of that information. The social psychologists in the sample did not describe in detail, as a group, any specific issues or concerns with how the world might interpret their work—this was seen as a necessary risk in the production of scientific knowledge. However, in thinking through the insights of the text network analysis, something that social psychologists might consider is the amendment or addition of a short statement to their publications, not too dissimilar from the current convention of adding a public impact statement to some academic publications. Perhaps if social psychologists offered a short citation statement or second, brief abstract at the beginning of every scientific article geared toward their nonacademic audiences who may seek to cite their work, it could give social psychologists some say in how the conclusions they make in their scientific reports are communicated out to the public by way of the consequential textual intermediaries discussed in this dissertation (e.g., Supreme Court briefs or journalistic coverage). These preliminary data offer initial insights into the conditions under which certain forms of psychological translation are engaged by authors of nonacademic texts and thus capacitate recommendations for how social psychologists might respond to the very real ways their work is being used.

The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is the development of portable technology solutions to allow Americans with disabilities to interact with the environment around them to increase their freedom and mobility. According to the Centers for Disease Control (CDC), 26% of Americans have a disability.  Current assistive technology is limited in what it can do because of the constrained processing powers that may be fitted in the confines of a portable device.  The proposed technology provides a means for transferring heavy processing to cloud-based servers that can draw on sufficient power to do the necessary work on a continual basis. The individual devices will be combinable and customizable in order to meet the individual needs off each user and to allow for maximum usability and value.  Technologies currently exist to aid people with disabilities to interact with their environment, however, the uptake of these devices has been very limited. The goal of this project will be to identify the reasons for this gap and use the data to ensure solutions meet the needs of the disabled community. The proposed solution will create individualized personal environmental support for the users to improve their mobility.

This I-Corps project is based on the development of advanced technologies in 5G, the Internet of Things (IoTs) and smart city applications. Currently, many cities have taken on smart city and urban computing initiatives where a set of disjointed sensor networks have been deployed in various parts of the city. These include: motion sensors, video cameras, biological sensors, audio recorders, fire detectors, gunshot location systems, and other monitoring tools.  The proposed technology is based on a cyber-physical system framework to bridge the physical space, cyberspace infused and Internet of Things (IoT). For example, people with vision loss or other special needs may have difficulties in perceiving signals directly in physical space, but they may be able to make these connections in cyberspace. These cyber connections and real-time information exchanges may enable and enhance their interactions in the physical space and allow them to be more aware of the environment around them.  This project may be accomplished by integrating existing technologies and commercialized electronics, such as a 5G network, WIFI, GPS, computer vision and a wider range of sensor devices.

According to a recent report by CDC Vision Health Initiative (VHI), approximately 12 million people 40 years and over in the United States have vision impairment. Vision disability is one of the top 10 disabilities among adults 18 years and older and one of the most prevalent disabling conditions among children. Vision loss causes a substantial social and economic toll for millions of people including significant suffering, disability, loss of productivity, and diminished quality of life. 

There are several fundamental issues that exist in many products on the market today, namely affordability, universal design and user interactability. There issues limited the wide adaption of these products by people with disabilities, especially, people with vision problems. 

The project goal is to develop and commercialize assistive technology (AT) based solutions for Americans with vision impairments to safely and effectively navigate unfamiliar places. Such technology solutions must be affordable, user friendly and acceptable to the intended customers. The solutions should help visually impaired people to increase independence, self-respect, and self-determination, therefore to make our society more inclusive.

Here are the major project outcomes and finds durating the award period:

1. We learned the scientific processes of customer discover that transformed ourselves from technology centric mindset to customer/market centric mindset. Our team learned and practiced the best business practices of customer discovery and business model development following the BMC (Business Model Canvas) method and using the LPC (LaunchPad Central). 

2. We completed the I-Corps training program during the 2021 Winter  with over 100 interviews - All our team members fully participated the training program curriculum and activities.   Among the interviewees, 70% are people with visual impairments and 30% are people who are working with visually impaired people, include,   product/service providers, NGO/Nonprofit advocacy organizations, and ADA (American Disability Acts) officers in universities/institutions.  

3. We indentified a set of core functions as our proposaed minimum viable product (MVP) with narrowed docus on O&M (orientation and mobility) in the areas of public transportation and access to common places, like transportation hubs, shopping centers, museums and college campuses.  

4. Our project provided opportunities of entrepreneur education to graduate students, especially, how to do customer/market discovery and transfer innovative technology from research lab to commercialized product. In addition, we provided the student training and hands on experiences about MVP product development from understand customer needs to design a cloud based mobile application.

5. One of our key findings is that we failed to validate our initial design approach which is based on “Smart Environment and Smart Agent” concept. In this design, the smart environment component requires onsite hardware/software installations for our product to work. We interviewed many facility owners and operators who rejected this design due to the installation cost and ongoing burden of maintenance. We went through a rethinking, pivot and redesign process to came up a new design approach for our proposed product, “ACloud-Based Assistive Mobile App to Aid People with Vision Impairments”, which does not need on site hardware/software. The cloud provides all the information processing functions equivalent to a smart environment with little or no cost to endusers. We revalidated the new design approach through another round of interviews. 

6. Another important finding is we reached a conclusion that the market for our product, with features specially designed for people with vision problem, has scalability problems, therefore, it is not sustainable.  We have to pivot and to change our design  focusing on universal design.  In addition, we have started to explore the possibility  to integrate our software based solutions with some of the products currently on the market. This is an OEM approach to increase marketability.

7. Based what we have learned from the customer discovery process, we have started to design and develop a proof concept prototype with the following design approach:

  • It is a lightweight mobile app that runs on smart phones so that users do not need to purchase any additional devices and hardware. It is affordable and it does not make the users stand out from the general population, since all people, include people with disabilities, own a smart phone already.
  • It is a cloud-based solution that lifts off heavy data processing and computing tasks from smart phones. Users have theflexibility to set up their mobile app in such a way to only enable the functions and the resolution scales that match their needs according to their disability profiles.
  • It integrates current available 5G and AI/machine learning technologies to utilize massive data on the cloud, so that it can learn the mobility  patterns over time from other people with similar disability need at same locations.
  • We plan to use Google Marketplace or Apple Store to distribute our mobile app distribution channels to reduce the development and distribution costs.

Adult language learners, including college students, find learning new languages to be difficult, yet many are remarkably successful. While previous work has focused on cognitive abilities (e.g. fluid intelligence, phonological short-term memory, declarative memory) as indicators of language learning aptitude, less attention has been given to how specific learning tasks might promote language learning in adults. Using a computer-assisted language learning (CALL) protocol, this project introduces an unfamiliar language to college students while varying learning tasks across participant groups. After listening to question-answer dialogues in the novel language, learners are prompted either to generate answers to the questions (i.e. brief phrases in the language), repeat answers to the questions, or answer forced-choice comprehension questions. The impacts on the learning outcomes of the different tasks are measured and assessed. Sessions are conducted remotely and recorded using web-based tools. 

Based on work in cognitive psychology demonstrating benefits of retrieval practice for learning, this project hypothesizes that adults who generate answers will outperform the other groups on tests assessing their comprehension of specific grammatical features of the new language, after controlling for individual differences in aptitude. Researchers hypothesize that after only two CALL sessions, adult learners will show neural markers associated with processing the grammatical structures (i.e. event-related potentials time-locked to errors) that will correlate with comprehension accuracy. Identification of the benefits of retrieval practice for comprehension will inform language learning instruction and aid in the development of effective web and mobile applications. The research will be conducted at a large urban public university with women and members of underrepresented groups involved as key personnel and participants.

How adults go about practicing a new language plays a role in their success in learning it.  Research in educational and cognitive psychology indicates that practice tests are important in strengthening memory. Our project examined how the format of practice tests, i.e., whether they require matching words to pictures or retrieving and saying the words from memory, influences language learning outcomes. Other research suggests that speaking aloud facilitates language learning. Hence, we also explored whether learners benefit equally from listening and repeating words from the new language (i.e., with no testing component) as compared to attempting to retrieve them from memory and then producing them aloud (i.e., a recall-based practice test).

In computer-assisted language learning sessions conducted on Zoom, adults learned a miniature version of Turkish as a new language. We introduced a vocabulary of Turkish nouns inflected for number (singular, plural) and case (dative [towards], ablative [away from]) in spoken question-answer dialogues. Specific learning tasks, requiring participants to speak aloud and/or complete practice tests, varied across groups. Speaking tasks involved listening and repeating Turkish words or recalling the words from memory and producing them aloud. Practice tests required recognition (select the corresponding picture) or recall (produce the Turkish word). After one hour of exposure to the Turkish dialogues and varied learning tasks, participants were tested on their comprehension of the Turkish vocabulary and grammatical patterns and asked to report what they had noticed about the language. 

Adults were more successful in learning Turkish vocabulary when the tasks required them to speak aloud, as compared to a learning condition where they never produced the words aloud (i.e., recognition-based tests). Moreover, their accuracy in repeating the inflected nouns on the first attempt predicted their vocabulary comprehension at the end of the session, as well as their grasp of Turkish case and number marking. Adults were more successful in learning the Turkish grammatical patterns after completing recognition- or recall-based practice tests. They were also better at learning case marking than plural marking, indicating the increased salience of grammatical markers at the ends of words. Individual differences in learning outcomes were associated with nonverbal ability, but not with language background or bilingualism. 

We also examined whether adult learners develop explicit awareness of what they are learning or whether it is possible for learners to develop good comprehension skills without being able to describe what they have learned. Most participants developed some explicit awareness of Turkish grammatical patterns as their comprehension skills improved. However, some learners demonstrated accurate comprehension without expressing any awareness of the grammar.  As pedagogical recommendations, we suggest that instructors should encourage language learners to speak aloud to strengthen word representations. Both recognition- and recall-based tests are effective in supporting learning of grammatical patterns and may promote meta-lingustic awareness.

In a follow up study using a picture-word verification task, we examined EEG correlates of error detection in adult learners and fluent speakers of Turkish. Prior to the EEG session, the learners completed two computer-assisted language learning sessions where they heard the Turkish nouns in spoken dialogues with recall or recognition-based practice tests. In the EEG session, nouns appeared in syntactic contexts (inflected for dative or ablative case) or in citation (nominative) forms. Both groups showed an increased negativity to semantic errors (N400) with an extended time course; however, the N400 was smaller in magnitude in learners compared to fluent speakers. Further analyses will examine ERPs in response to case and number errors as indicators of grammatical sensitivity. Our preliminary analyses suggest that neural markers of vocabulary comprehension are robust, even at earliest stages of language learning, whereas markers of grammatical processing are more difficult to detect in adult learners.

Indigenous peoples are developing novel social mechanisms to deal with rapid change and emerging conflicts, including land resettlement, language revitalization and traditional skill-building. However, we know little about the processes and contexts from which these strategies arise.

This project will use a case study from the Northwest Coast of North America to evaluate how Indigenous communities socially and culturally adapt to conflicts over sovereignty, land use and access. This research aims to document the new social networks that emerge in these contexts and how they contribute to Indigenous resiliency. To understand the opportunities and consequences of emerging networks, this project will (1) document the socio-cultural norms that emerge amidst Indigenous resettlement of traditional territories; (2) identify types of social networks that develop; (3) evaluate connections between these new networks and gender, race, and economic factors.  The ultimate objective is to trace community networks and evaluate their impacts on Indigenous resilience, an issue with broad implications for Arctic Indigenous communities.

For this project, the researcher used the methodology of auto-ethnography to document their experience of an Indigenous land-defense encampment. Through active participant observation, historical research, and examination of media products during the course of the project, the research describes the historical and political context of current Wet'suwet'en land disputes, including the effects of environmental change, Canadian legal and political structures, and resource extraction on access to and use of Indigenous lands. The project juxtaposes the operational frameworks of resource extraction companies with Wet'suwet'en understandings of seasonality, land use, and Indigenous sovereignty. By analyzing how space is defined and understood by different actors in the dispute over pipeline construction, the research illuminates points of tension between Indigenous and corporate ways of knowing the environment and our place within it. 

This research methodology contributes to an Indigenous feminist approach by working from the experience and perspective of the researcher. Auto-ethnography is an important method within anthropology and related fields, and the narrative style of the completed dissertation provides a model for social science inquiry firmly embedded in Indigenous worldviews and protocols. The analysis shows how resource extraction constrains the use of land for Wet'suwet'en people, and has broad applicability in human geography, Indigenous studies, and anthropology. Additionally, the research utilizes the framework of Indigenous environmental justice to demonstrate how colonial histories and contexts continue to affect the current experience of land-based politics, climate change, cultural practices, and relationships to the environment for Indigenous peoples. As such, it is also applicable to environmental policy and management, Indigenous governance and Canadian legal mechanisms, and organizations working in environmental justice and Indigenous rights.

abstractText:
In the sciences in general, the phrase “route to chaos” has come to refer to a metaphor when some physical, biological, economic, or social system transitions from one exhibiting order to one displaying randomness (or chaos). The goal of this project is to understand which universal mechanisms explain that transition, and how one can describe systems that operate in a region between order and complete chaos, where the complexity is maximal. In other words, the goal is to understand the processes by which a system evolves from periodic toward chaotic behavior as one or more parameters governing the behavior of the system are varied. This has only been understood in low dimensional dynamics (which are as simple as a system involving one variable). The present project presents a novel approach that allows us to move away from those limitations. Moreover, the project brings some perspectives to new advances in mathematics and science in general, not necessarily in terms of bringing techniques or theorems, but in terms of ideas and conceptual approaches. The project will also support the training of graduate students, directly involved in this research.


The current project presents a tentative global framework toward describing a large class of area contracting surface dynamics of the disc with zero and low entropy, inspired partially by the developments in the one-dimensional theory of interval maps. More precisely, the project proposes a class of intermediate smooth dynamics between one and higher dimensions (that includes the Henon family with Jacobian smaller than 1 /4 ) where it could be possible to develop a similar one-dimensional type approach that could help to understand dynamics with zero or low topological entropy. In particular, it presents a general framework to understand the transition from zero entropy to positive entropy.

Abstract

Artificial intelligence (AI) has many impressive applications, including self-driving cars, computer vision, and speech recognition. This project demonstrates that many challenging economic models and applications can be successfully analyzed by using the same break-ground AI technologies and the same state-of-the-art combinations of software and hardware as those used by data scientists for dealing with their impressive applications. This project develops open-source AI software that makes it possible to examine complex economic models that were intractable under the earlier solution methods. Applications of this AI framework include central-banking models of monetary policy, growth models of wealth inequality, and models of social security and population aging. The developed AI tools will be disseminated in the profession by providing carefully documented replicated materials, examples and tutorials.

This project consists of several components. First, the project shows how to convert three fundamental objects of economic dynamics -- lifetime reward, Bellman equation and Euler equation -- into objective functions suitable for deep learning. Second, the project adapts the stochastic gradient descent method to maximizing the objective on few randomly drawn grid points instead of a large fixed grid used by conventional solution methods. Third, the project shows how to construct the expectation operators for dynamic economic models by combining multiple expectation operators into a single unbiased expectation operator. Fourth, the project automates the AI solution framework to make it ubiquitous and portable to other applications. Fifth, the project solves a collection of empirically relevant applications that represent challenges to the existing solution methods in economics.

projectOutComesReport:
Final outcomes.  Our AI analysis has key four ingredients for dealing with the curse of dimensionality. Our first ingredient is a neural network. A biological neuron consists of a cell body connected to other neurons through input dendrites and output axons. An artificial neuron mimics a biological neuron: inputs x=(x₁,...,x_{n}) weighted by the coefficients w=(w₁,...,w_{n}) are transformed via an activation function to produce an output, see Figure 1.

    Artificial neurons are combined into multiple layers. The network provides a flexible functional form capable of approximating highly nonlinear complex objects. Moreover, neural networks performs model reduction: it condenses information from a large number of inputs into a smaller number of neurons in the hidden layers without losing essential information. This is similar to photo compression.    Our second ingredient is a random grid constructed using simulated series (ergodic set). The economic literature generally solves the models on prespecified hypercube domains. Stochastic simulation typically have a shape of a hypersphere (hyperoval) like the one in Figure 2.

    The ratio of a volume of a hypersphere to the volume of an enclosing hypercube is an infinitesimally small number in high-dimensional applications; for example, with 30 dimensions, this ratio is of order 10⁻¹⁴. Thus, restricting domain to the area in which the solution "lives" reduces the cost enormously.    Our third ingredient is an AI classification method for constructing discrete-set choices. As an illustration, let us consider the image recognition problem, for example, a machine classifies images into cats, dogs and sheep. We parameterize the probabilities of the three classes with a neural network. The machine is given a collection of images and is trained to minimize the cross-entropy loss that ensures the correct classification of images, see Figure 3.

    Our classification method in economics works in the same way. For example, in a model with three indivisible labor choices, we parameterize the probabilities of being full-time employed, part-time employed and unemployed. The machine is given employment choices and is trained to maximize the likelihood function that make those choices optimal. The same idea can be applied for analyzing other discrete choices such as retirement, default, house purchase, etc.    Our last novel ingredient is an all-in-one expectation operator that combines multiple expectation operators into a single one making high-dimensional integration tractable. In Figure 4, we illustrate an example of training under the proposed operator.

    In left panel, we see the reduction in approximation errors; and in right panel, we see the evolution of decision rules when the machine learns to approximate the kink.    Taken together our ingredients enable us to solve models with dimensionality and complexity intractable up to now. Our results are shown in four subprojects. In subproject 1, we introduce an AI framework for analyzing dynamic economic models. In subproject 2, we solve a large-scale new Keynesian ToTEM model of the Bank of Canada. In Subproject 3, we extend our AI solution approach to include mixed discrete-continuous choices. Finally, in Subproject 4, we solve a challenging class new Keynesian models with a continuum of heterogeneous agents and stochastic idiosyncratic volatility. We also assess the implications of automatic stabilization policies in light of the COVID pandemic.

The project has multiple broader impacts: First, the results of the project were presented on 35 conferences and seminars and led to five articles, three of which are published in leading international journals. Second, the developed AI tools are not limited to macroeconomics but can be applied to literally any field both within and outside economics that uses dynamic stochastic models. Third, the applications analyzed in the project are of considerable interest on their own. In particular, the analysis of the large-scale ToTEM model can contribute to better understanding of the current and past economic crises as well as suggest government policies that can prevent or mitigate the economic downturns in the future. Furthermore, the new studied Keynesian model with heterogeneous agents can help us in designing differential economic policies targeting certain social groups. Fourth, we made our teaching materials, computer codes and the data available to researchers including underrepresented groups. Fifth, the project contributed to teaching and mentoring graduate and undergraduate students. In particular, four undergraduate students of Santa Clara University and four graduate students of Columbia University were hired and trained. The outcomes of the project were presented in numerous minicourses in both the US and international institutions: Columbia University, Rice University, Baruch College, Stony Brook University, Bank of Chile, Peking University, Bank of Canada, University of Texas at Austin. Finally, the proposed framework can be used by public and private institutions, including the US government agencies and US Fed for economic modeling, optimal policy choice and economics forecasts. Currently, the Bank of Canada is incorporating our AI analysis for constructing reliable nonlinear solutions to their ToTEM model for projection and policy analysis.
